THE HAGUE, Netherlands – On Monday, November 30, former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is set to begin trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) over alleged crimes against humanity relating to his bloody drug war in the Philippines.

The much-anticipated trial phase is when the parties in the case, namely, the ICC prosecutor, the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRV), and Duterte’s defense team, will present evidence and witness testimonies.

Unlike the confirmation of charges hearing last February, when the pre-trial chamber’s goal was to determine whether there was sufficient evidence in the prosecution’s case to proceed to trial, the judges in Trial Chamber III will now determine whether Duterte is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.

The crimes were alleged to have been committed during Duterte’s anti-illegal drug operations as Davao City mayor and vice mayor, utilizing his so-called Davao Death Squad, as well as when he replicated the Davao model on a nationwide scale upon assuming the presidency in 2016.
Here’s what to expect when trial begins.
When trial opens, the judges will ask Duterte whether he understands the charges filed against him and ask him to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty.
The equivalent of this in the Philippine legal process is called an arraignment.
The ICC prosecutor and the victims’ representatives are expected to deliver opening statements after Duterte enters a plea. These are expected to take several hours each.
The defense will deliver a short introduction of its case, but a longer opening statement is expected later in the trial.

blocks.caption: Duterte’s drug war was state-sanctioned, killed over 8,000 – Truth Commission

blocks.text: After the opening statements, the prosecution will begin presenting its witnesses. In the first weeks of the trial, that is, before the court goes on its winter recess on December 18, the prosecution is expected to present five witnesses.
The prosecution expects to present around 100 witnesses over the course of the trial.

“As with other complex cases involving allegations of crimes against humanity, these proceedings are expected to take some time. The exact duration of the trial will depend on a number of factors, including the volume of evidence, the number of witnesses, and any procedural matters that may arise during the trial,” said ICC spokesperson Oriane Huber Maillet in a briefing with reporters on Tuesday, November 24.
Only after the prosecution presents its case will the defense have the opportunity to present theirs.
The ICC presumes Duterte to be innocent unless and until proven guilty before the court.

“He is represented by counsel of his choosing and is entitled to all fair trial guarantees provided under the Rome Statute, including adequate time and facilities to prepare his defense, the ability to challenge the Prosecution’s evidence, and the opportunity to present evidence and witnesses on his own behalf,” said Maillet.
More than 500 victims of extrajudicial killings in Duterte’s drug war are authorized to participate in the trial through their team of legal representatives.
The ICC said it was taking steps to protect victims and witnesses from threats against their well-being.
ICC hearings are public and can be followed in two ways: in person, by attending the hearings at the ICC’s headquarters in The Hague, or online via its Facebook and YouTube channels.

Viewers in the public gallery can watch the proceedings live, while online streams will have a 30-minute delay to allow for redactions in the event that confidential information is divulged during open session. The judges will occasionally call for a closed session to protect confidential information or participants.

“The Court remains committed to ensuring that these proceedings are conducted fairly, independently and transparently, in accordance with the Rome Statute and the Court’s legal framework,” said Maillet.
Both the pro- and anti-Duterte camps are expected to stage their own events and demonstrations in the days leading up to trial and when it begins.

On November 30, the Duterte Panagutin Network will hold a march and protest on ICC grounds, just before trial starts at 9 am. From 10 am onwards, Duterte’s supporters are expected to occupy the area in front of the ICC to stage their demonstration.
The ICC is set to begin Duterte’s trial amid a sharp delegitimization campaign from the former president’s supporters and global superpowers like the United States.

“The Court’s role is not to pursue any political objective. Rather, its role is to determine, through independent and impartial judicial proceedings, whether the charges have been proven according to the law,” said Maillet. – Rappler.com
